title: Design a URL Shortener
oneLiner: A full 45-minute design round for bit.ly, stage by stage: write your answer, then compare it with a strong one.
keyTakeaway: A URL shortener is a read-dominated key-value lookup, so the design is about making redirects cache hits and generating short, unique, non-sequential codes without coordinating on every write. Interviewers grade the trade-offs you say out loud (hash vs counter vs leased ID ranges, 301 vs 302) more than the boxes you draw.
explanation:
This is a practice run of a real system design interview. The widget plays the interviewer: it gives you the prompt, then walks through the seven stages a 45-minute round usually follows. In each stage, write your own answer in the box first, the way you would say it out loud, and only then press "Compare with the model answer". Tick the points you genuinely covered. The score is for you; nobody else sees it, and your notes stay in this browser.

Writing first matters. Reading a model answer feels like understanding, but in the interview you have to produce the answer from a blank whiteboard, under time pressure, while someone watches. Comparing your own attempt with a strong one shows you exactly what you forgot, and the gaps are usually the same few things: no numbers, no stated trade-off, no failure modes.

The usual flow, with rough timings: about 5 minutes on requirements (ask questions, split functional from non-functional, say what's out of scope), 4 on back-of-the-envelope estimation, 4 on the API, 5 on the data model and storage choice, 8 on the high-level design, about 15 on deep dives into the hard parts, and the last 4 on bottlenecks, failure modes and monitoring. The first five minutes of a real interview go on introductions and the last five on your questions, which is why the design itself has to fit in about 35 to 45. Running out of time before the deep dives is the most common way to fail: the deep dives are where senior candidates are separated from junior ones.

What interviewers grade, roughly in this order. First, whether you clarified the problem instead of designing the first thing that came to mind: scale, read/write ratio, what "done" means. Second, whether you state trade-offs out loud: every choice (a 302 instead of a 301, a key-value store instead of SQL) should come with what it costs you and why that's acceptable here. Third, numbers: requests per second, storage, cache size, and the design decision each number leads to. Fourth, how you handle follow-ups: when the interviewer says "what if one link gets 1 million clicks a minute?", they want to see you reason from the design you drew, not start over. There is no single correct design; there are well-argued ones.

The URL shortener is the classic warm-up problem because the happy path is easy and the depth is in the details: how to make 7-character codes unique without a global lock, why sequential codes are a privacy problem, what browser caching of a 301 does to your analytics, and how one viral link can melt a single cache shard. The model answer uses 100 million new links a day and a 100:1 read ratio, the numbers most interviewers expect you to assume if they don't give you any.

Use "Start over" to clear your notes and try again a week later; spaced repetition of a full round is the most effective preparation there is. Once you can do this one comfortably inside 45 minutes, move on to the news feed and chat walk-throughs, which reuse the same building blocks under much harder constraints.
